pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied aphids cluster on growing tips and the undersides of leaves, often where leaves meet the stem, causing curling, yellowing, and sticky honeydew followed by sooty mold. Heavy feeding stunts young plants, and several aphid species also transmit mosaic viruses.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft insects gather on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, making the leaves curl and turn yellow, often with a sticky film. You may see ants tending them.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species feed on okra by sucking sap, building up fast in warm weather and especially on soft, over-fertilized growth. The honeydew they excrete fosters sooty mold and draws ants.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck the plant's juices and multiply quickly in warm weather, particularly on soft growth from too much nitrogen.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water, then spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout growing tips and leaf undersides regularly, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves often, and let helpful insects do their work instead of spraying everything.

pests.name: Corn earworm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Caterpillars chew into buds, flowers, and developing pods, leaving holes and frass, and feeding can deform or ruin the tender pods okra is grown for. The same species (Helicoverpa zea) attacks corn and tomato, so pressure is high where those crops are nearby.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Caterpillars eat into the okra buds, flowers, and young pods, leaving holes and droppings and ruining the pods. They are the same worms that get into corn ears and tomatoes.
pests.cause_seasoned: The corn earworm, larva of the moth Helicoverpa zea, lays eggs on the plant in summer; the hatching larvae bore into buds and pods. There can be several overlapping generations through the season in the South.
pests.cause_beginner: A moth lays eggs on the plant in summer, and the caterpillars that hatch bore into the buds and pods. There can be several rounds of them over a season.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Scout buds and pods and hand-pick larvae, harvest pods frequently so fewer are exposed, and treat young larvae with Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) or spinosad, covering buds and developing pods where the caterpillars feed.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the caterpillars off by hand, keep harvesting pods often, and spray a caterpillar-specific product like Bt on the buds and young pods if they are a problem.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout from first flowering, pick pods every day or two to remove feeding sites, encourage natural enemies, and avoid planting okra immediately beside corn, which shares and amplifies this pest.
pests.prevention_beginner: Start checking when the plant begins to flower, harvest often, and try not to plant okra right next to corn, since they share this pest.

pests.name: Stink bugs and leaf-footed bugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Shield-shaped stink bugs and narrow leaf-footed bugs pierce pods to feed, leaving sunken, warty, or discolored spots and causing crooked, distorted growth. Damage concentrates on the pods, which are the harvested part.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Shield-shaped or narrow brown bugs feed on the pods, leaving dimpled, warty, or twisted spots. The pods may grow crooked where they have fed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several true bugs, including the southern green stink bug and leaf-footed bugs, feed with piercing-sucking mouthparts on okra pods through the summer, building up in weedy borders and on nearby legumes.
pests.cause_beginner: These bugs pierce the pods and suck out the juices, which deforms them. They build up over summer, often coming in from weeds and nearby beans or peas.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults and crush egg masses in the cool of the morning when bugs are sluggish, knock them into soapy water, and treat hot spots with insecticidal soap on nymphs, which are easier to kill than adults. A cowpea trap planting concentrates them for removal.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the bugs off into soapy water, especially early in the morning when they are slow, and scrape off egg clusters. Young bugs are easier to treat with insecticidal soap than the adults.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep weedy borders mowed to cut harborage, scout pods and leaf undersides for egg masses from early summer, harvest frequently, and use a cowpea trap crop to pull bugs off the okra.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep weeds down around the patch, check the pods and leaves for eggs through the summer, and harvest often. A row of cowpeas nearby can draw the bugs away.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny shiny beetles chew small round shot-holes in the leaves, worst on young plants and seedlings; established okra tolerates the cosmetic damage, but heavy early feeding can set back seedlings.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny dark beetles chew lots of small round holes in the leaves, especially on young plants. They jump away when you get close.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several flea beetle species feed on okra foliage, most active in spring and early summer on tender young growth. Mature plants generally outgrow the damage.
pests.cause_beginner: Small jumping beetles that chew tiny holes in leaves. They are most active in spring on young plants, which are the most vulnerable.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with floating row cover until they are established and growing strongly, dust with diatomaceous earth, and tolerate light feeding on robust plants, which seldom needs treatment.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover until they are bigger, and do not worry about a few holes on a strong, growing plant.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Sow into warm soil for fast, vigorous emergence, keep seedlings growing without check, and clear weedy hosts nearby; healthy okra quickly grows past the vulnerable stage.
pests.prevention_beginner: Plant when the soil is warm so seedlings grow fast and strong, and keep weeds down. Healthy plants soon grow past the stage where flea beetles matter.

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants yellow and wilt, often one side first, with lower leaves dying upward and stunted growth; a cut stem shows brown streaking in the water-conducting tissue. Infected plants decline through the season and may collapse.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plant yellows and wilts, sometimes one side at a time, and the lower leaves die first. If you cut the stem you see brown streaks inside. It slowly weakens the plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne Fusarium fungus that enters through the roots and clogs the vascular system, favored by warm soil. It persists in the soil for years and is shared with other Malvaceae such as cotton.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soilborne fungus that infects the roots and blocks the plant's water pipes, so it wilts. It lives in the soil for years and also affects okra's relatives like cotton.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy affected plants to limit buildup. Management is preventive and cultural: it cannot be sprayed out of the soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. You cannot spray it away once it is in the soil.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate okra out of the bed for several years and away from cotton and other mallows, choose tolerant varieties where available, plant in well-drained soil, and manage root-knot nematodes, which open the way for wilt.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Move okra to a fresh spot each year and keep it away from cotton and hibiscus, plant in well-drained soil, and control root-knot nematodes, which make wilt worse.

diseases.name: Southern blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A sudden wilt and collapse of the plant, with a soft, brown rot at the stem base near the soil line. In warm, humid weather you see a white, fan-like fungal mat and small tan, mustard-seed-sized resting bodies (sclerotia) around the crown.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plant wilts and collapses, with a soft rotten spot at the base of the stem. You may see white fuzzy growth and tiny tan balls like mustard seeds at the soil line.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The soilborne fungus Sclerotium rolfsii, which thrives in hot, humid weather and attacks the stem base, especially where organic debris sits against the stem. Its sclerotia survive in soil for years.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soilborne fungus that loves hot, humid weather and rots the base of the stem. It survives in the soil and in old plant debris for years.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for a collapsed plant; remove and destroy it along with the surrounding infested soil crust. Keep mulch and debris pulled back from the stem base to slow spread.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure for an infected plant, so remove it and the soil right around its base. Keep mulch and old leaves away from the stems.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate with non-host crops such as grasses and corn, bury or remove crop debris that feeds the fungus, improve drainage, space for airflow, and avoid piling mulch against the stems.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rotate okra with crops like corn, clean up old plant debris, plant in well-drained soil with room for air, and keep mulch off the stems.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White, powdery patches develop on leaf surfaces, mostly later in the season, spreading until leaves yellow and dry. Early defoliation reduces the plant's vigor and can shorten the productive run of pods.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white, powdery coating spreads over the leaves, usually later in the season, until they yellow and dry up. The plant fades and makes fewer pods.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Powdery mildew fungi that thrive in warm conditions with high humidity but do not need leaf wetness, spreading by wind-blown spores. Crowding, poor airflow, and shade worsen it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads on warm, humid days, especially where plants are crowded and air does not move well. It does not need wet leaves to take hold.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Treat at the first spots with a labeled fungicide such as sulfur, horticultural oil, or a biofungicide, covering both leaf surfaces, and remove the worst leaves. Avoid overhead watering.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Treat early, at the first white spots, with a labeled fungicide like sulfur or horticultural oil, and remove badly affected leaves. Water the soil, not the leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants generously for airflow, plant in full sun, avoid excess nitrogen and overhead watering, and scout from midseason so you can treat at the first sign.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants plenty of room, plant in full sun, water at the base, and start checking in midsummer so you catch it early.

diseases.name: Root-knot nematode
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants are stunted, yellowed, and prone to midday wilting even with adequate water; pulling a plant reveals knots and galls swelling the roots. Okra is highly susceptible, and galled roots cannot take up water and nutrients well, opening the way for fusarium wilt.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plant is stunted and yellow and wilts in the heat even when watered. If you dig it up, the roots have knots and swellings on them. Okra is very prone to this one.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Microscopic soilborne root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne species) that infect roots and form galls, building up in sandy soils and persisting on many host crops and weeds. Okra is among their most susceptible hosts.
diseases.cause_beginner: Tiny soil worms that attack the roots and make knots on them, which keeps the plant from drinking and feeding properly. They build up in the soil, especially sandy soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no in-season cure; remove and destroy heavily galled plants and their roots. Management is preventive, through rotation, resistant crops, and soil organic matter that supports nematode antagonists.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once roots are knotted, so pull and destroy badly affected plants and their roots. The fix is preventing them next season.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate to poor hosts such as grains and certain marigold cover crops, solarize infested beds in summer, add organic matter, control host weeds, and avoid following okra with cotton or other susceptible Malvaceae.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Move okra to a fresh spot, grow a nematode-suppressing cover crop like certain marigolds, add compost, keep weeds down, and do not plant okra where it or cotton grew last year.
